title: A short distance to a 1 C warmer climate did not improve bird thermal tracking on 3,960 US survey routes (1966-2025); colonisation fell with distance but local warming did not direct it
abstract: Question: the bird community temperature index (CTI) of North American Breeding Bird Survey (BBS) routes follows only a small part of its spatial temperature slope in time. Is the gap set by colonisation distance, that is, by how far a route is from a climate that is 1 C warmer? Data: 107,922 standard BBS runs on 3,960 contiguous-US routes (467 species, 1966-2025), NOAA nClimGrid monthly mean temperature and precipitation (about 5 km), USFS forest type map. Method (plan written before outcomes): analog distance D1 from each route to the nearest 1 C warmer 1966-1995 May-July climate (median 101 km East, 17 km West of 100 W); cross-fitted CTI; tracking fraction O/E by D1 tercile inside each region (observed trend with route and observer effects over the trend expected from the local spatial slope and route warming); within 4 degree block x year contrasts; 100-draw block bootstrap. Results: O/E was 0.22, 0.18, 0.36 (East) and 0.55, 0.55, 0.94 (West) from short to long distance. The fraction did not fall with distance, and in no bootstrap draw did short-distance routes track 2 times better. The raw within-block contrast was positive (+0.0064 C per decade per SD of log D1); after forest share, baseline temperature and warming controls it was -0.0005 (SE 0.0016), outside the 2:1 predictions (-0.0069 East, -0.0133 West). Distance thresholds of 0.5 and 2 C, gradient velocity, thermal heterogeneity, regional year effects and period changes gave the same result. Exploratory: colonisation probability fell from 15-25% (source under 25 km) to under 0.5% (over 400 km), but warmer species colonised only 1.2-1.5 times as often as colder ones, and this warm bias did not grow with route warming. National species trends on fixed species sets gave 23% of the CTI trend; local warming rate did not predict the route CTI trend. The invasive Eurasian Collared-Dove gave about 20% of the West trend in a first-order split. Conclusion: arrival distance does not set the bird thermal-tracking gap; the limit is at establishment, or the spatial benchmark is not causal. Limitations: correlational; the result depends on forest and temperature controls; climate distance is not habitat distance; the colonisation and species analyses are exploratory.

display.caption: Tracking fraction (observed / expected CTI trend) by tercile of distance to a 1 C warmer climate, East and West of 100 W, with 95% block-bootstrap CIs. The dispersal-distance hypothesis predicts a fall from left to right; the data show no fall.

Within-block contrast of the CTI trend per 1 SD of each distance moderator in 10 specifications (95% CI). Dashed lines: size predicted if short-distance routes tracked 2 times better. The raw contrast is positive; after forest and temperature controls it is about zero.

Probability that a species absent from a route in 1966-1985 was established in 2006-2025, by distance to the nearest 1966-1985 source route and by species temperature index relative to the route. Colonisation falls with distance; warm species are favoured only a little.
